status: Pre-filing / intake stage — newly enrolled CASOMB-certified sex offender treatment program in San Jose following the July 2, 2026 retaliatory parole transfer to Santa Clara County. Pleading framework mirrors Matter 28 (NDCA HOPE action) and Matter 5 (state tort / institutional fraud), targeting containment-model retention policies, fee-for-service structural conflicts, and compliance monitoring under 15 CCR §3574.
key_facts: Following the July 2, 2026 retaliatory transfer of parole supervision from San Joaquin County to the Santa Clara County Parole GPS Unit (the subject of Matter 30), Plaintiff was mandated by CDCR parole to enroll in a new CASOMB-certified sex offender treatment program in San Jose, California. The Counseling and Psychotherapy Center, Inc. (d/b/a CPC / CPC America) is a private forensic mental health contractor operating specialized containment-model treatment programs across multiple states and Northern California locations, including San Jose, Oakland, Sacramento, Modesto, Fresno, Salinas, and Monterey. As a CDCR-contracted provider exercising delegated state authority over mandatory conditions of parole, CPC and its clinical administrators operate as state actors under color of state law for constitutional purposes under West v. Atkins, 487 U.S. 42 (1988). Matter 34 is scaffolded as the prospective companion/successor action to Matter 5 (San Joaquin Sup. Ct. state tort / fraud action, dismissed on exhaustion grounds July 15, 2026) and Matter 28 (USDC N.D. Cal. §1983 / Monell / RICO action, filed July 20, 2026), both of which targeted HOPE Psychotherapy, Inc. for institutional blanket-retention practices judicially condemned in In re Dwyer (San Mateo County Super. Ct., Mar. 20, 2023). Matter 34 monitors and investigates CPC's intake procedures, treatment agreements, and clinical progress reporting under 15 CCR §3574(f)(1) and Penal Code §3008(d)(2), specifically evaluating: (1) whether CPC conceals an institutional policy of retaining parolees through the full duration of supervision regardless of objective clinical progress; (2) fee-for-service structural incentive misalignment where client-funded and state-funded session fees create financial incentives against timely treatment graduation; (3) CTM reporting practices on CDCR Form 3043 / Form 1502-DR; (4) interference with Class A commercial driver employment (prior documented losses of $109,408 across 2022–2024; $72,000/yr but-for earning capacity); and (5) coercive compliance conditioning actionable under the Bane Act (Civ. Code §52.1) and UCL §17200.
procedural_status: Pre-filing stage. Matter opened following Plaintiff's July/August 2026 post-transfer enrollment at CPC's San Jose facility to preserve and audit intake agreements, treatment rules, clinical orientation statements, and CDCR Form 3043 reporting. No complaint or Government Claim has yet been filed. Operative drafting will adapt the verified §1983 / Monell / Bane Act / Fraud pleading template established in Matter 28 (3:26-cv-07504) and Matter 5 (STK-CV-UF-2026-0001032), tailored to CPC's corporate structure (CEO Dennis McNamara, COO Kellie McNamara, CCO Maria Piccillo) and local San Jose clinical staff once identified through intake and discovery.
damages: Pre-filing / contingent valuation modeled on Matter 28: §1983 compensatory damages for liberty deprivation and constitutional harms; lost earning capacity and career displacement under Class A CDL ($72,000/yr but-for rate; documented $109,408+ prior losses); Bane Act statutory penalties ($25,000 per violation under Civ. Code §52.1); potential RICO treble damages under 18 U.S.C. §1964(c); UCL §17200 restitution of client-paid fees; punitive damages under Civ. Code §3294; and statutory attorney fees under 42 U.S.C. §1988 and CCP §1021.5.
risk: Pre-filing / investigatory posture: liability will depend on CPC's specific intake disclosures, written treatment contract, and whether CPC enforces an unlawful blanket-retention policy analogous to HOPE's in Dwyer. State-actor doctrine under West v. Atkins firmly established for CDCR-contracted treatment providers. Commercial driving accommodation and scheduling conflicts must be documented early. Coordination required with Matter 28 (HOPE NDCA) to maintain consistent legal arguments while avoiding damages overlap across different supervisory periods.
